title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
content:
Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.
The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”
“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.
Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.
But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.
Rising emissions
Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.
That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

report.summary: Meta is re-evaluating its 2030 net-zero timeline after AI data-center buildout drove record emissions growth, a notable retreat among Big Tech climate pledges.
report.background: Meta’s rethink arrives as the AI boom turns data centers into one of the tech industry’s fastest-growing sources of energy demand. Hyperscale campuses require enormous electricity for GPUs, cooling, and backup power, and construction and server manufacturing add “embodied” emissions before a facility ever runs. Meta and peers had pledged aggressive climate targets—often net zero across operations or value chains by 2030—while also racing to build AI capacity. Renewable procurement and grid upgrades have not kept pace with compute demand, so companies increasingly rely on natural-gas generation and face delays in clean-power interconnection. Sustainability reports are now a pressure point: investors, regulators, and customers compare emissions trajectories, even as AI competition rewards speed over decarbonization. Meta’s 2025 emissions jump illustrates how capital spending on servers and data centers can overwhelm efficiency gains.
key_points: Meta is formally re-evaluating the 2030 timeframe for its net-zero emissions goal and its near-term emissions-intensity targets. In its 2026 sustainability report, executives said long-term ambitions are unchanged, but AI infrastructure demand has grown faster than almost anyone projected, forcing a review of timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones.

Meta’s total greenhouse gas emissions rose from 15.6 million metric tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million in 2025. That is a record percentage increase among Big Tech firms, roughly equal to Idaho’s total emissions and more than Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, or New Hampshire. Meta mainly blamed capital goods such as data-center servers.

The disclosure stands out because Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have so far retained their original sustainability goals, even as all acknowledge tension between climate pledges and hyperscale AI buildouts. Companies continue investing in renewables, but many AI data centers still depend on natural gas, undercutting near-term decarbonization.

Meta says it will keep progress transparent year over year while revising milestones. The change matters because it creates a public template for adjusting climate targets when AI growth outpaces clean-energy supply, potentially giving rivals political cover to do the same.
report.impact: Meta’s admission reframes AI’s climate cost as a mainstream business risk, not a footnote. For the AI industry, it could weaken the credibility of 2030 net-zero pledges and shift scrutiny toward energy procurement, grid interconnection, and disclosure quality. Rivals may face investor and regulator questions if they keep targets unchanged while emissions rise. For developers, the signal is that compute efficiency, carbon-aware scheduling, and location choices increasingly matter alongside model performance; server and hardware lifecycles become part of the carbon problem. For regular users, AI products may carry a larger hidden environmental footprint, but better measurement and transparency could eventually drive greener defaults. The risk is that “re-evaluating timelines” becomes an industry norm, delaying decarbonization just as AI demand accelerates.
report.tools: To follow emissions from AI workloads, watch Cloud Carbon Footprint (open-source cloud emissions estimates), CodeCarbon (tracks compute emissions), Electricity Maps and WattTime (grid carbon intensity data), the Green Software Foundation’s SCI specification, and MLCommons MLPerf Power for energy-efficiency benchmarks. These help developers and sustainability teams connect AI compute to real energy use and carbon outcomes.
